brief: Morgan Stanley argues AI infrastructure is hitting a physical tipping point: the grid cannot deliver power fast enough, political pushback is making mega-campus data centers harder to site, and inference is shifting compute toward smaller nodes closer to users. Together these forces push the industry toward distributed, behind-the-meter (BTM) power rather than a few giant grid-dependent campuses. The firm forecasts 160 GW of incremental US data center demand through 2029 against 36 GW of available grid capacity and 23 GW of already-procured BTM equipment, leaving a 77 GW shortfall to be filled by fuel cells, gas turbines and reciprocating engines, implying a ~120 GW/$240bn BTM equipment TAM. It introduces the Stranded Compute Adjusted Cost of Power (SCACP), adding an idle-GPU opportunity cost to LCOE, and ranks Bloom Energy's SOFC #1, BorgWarner's turbine #2 and FTAI's aeroderivative #3 today; without the time-to-power premium the ranking shifts toward cheaper technologies by 2030. Growth in data-center BTM power is expected to lower costs and spill into C&I demand (40 GW by 2029) and reshoring. Storage and VPPs (Sunrun/Tesla) complement generation; political opposition adds further pressure favoring onsite power.
